title: On the Impossibility of SNARGs with Short CRS
authors: Liyan Chen (MIT, USA), Zhengzhong Jin (Northeastern University, USA)
abstract: We study the inherent barriers to constructing non-adaptively sound succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) for NP with a CRS whose length is sublinear in the witness length. Our results cover both the standard SNARGs and SNARGs with an additional updatable feature (i.e. incrementally verifiable computation for NP). • For updatable SNARGs, we show a black-box separation from falsifiable assumptions for uniform polynomial-time reductions, assuming sub-exponential hardness of learning with error. • For general SNARGs, we show a black-box separation from falsifiable assumptions for non-uniform polynomial-time reductions that only make one query to the adversary, assuming the existence of sub-exponentially secure super-bit generators. We observe that all known SNARG constructions from polynomial hardness of standard assumptions have 1-query soundness reductions. Thus, our result complements existing constructions. Previously, the seminal work [Gentry-Wichs, STOC11] showed a black-box separation of SNARGs from falsifiable assumptions in the adaptive soundness setting. We explore whether any barriers exist in the non-adaptive setting. To obtain our result, we derive a simulation lemma for unbounded polynomial-length auxiliary inputs assuming super-bit generators.

Abstract—We study the inherent barriers to constructing nonadaptively sound succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) for
NP with a CRS whose length is sublinear in the witness length.
Our results cover both the standard SNARGs and SNARGs
with an additional updatable feature (i.e. incrementally verifiable
computation for NP).
• For updatable SNARGs, we show a black-box separation
from falsifiable assumptions for uniform polynomial-time
reductions, assuming sub-exponential hardness of learning
with error.
• For general SNARGs, we show a black-box separation
from falsifiable assumptions for non-uniform polynomialtime reductions that only make one query to the adversary,
assuming the existence of sub-exponentially secure super-bit
generators. We observe that all known SNARG constructions
from polynomial hardness of standard assumptions have
1-query soundness reductions. Thus, our result complements
existing constructions.
Previously, the seminal work [Gentry-Wichs, STOC’11] showed
a black-box separation of SNARGs from falsifiable assumptions in
the adaptive soundness setting. We explore whether any barriers
exist in the non-adaptive setting. To obtain our result, we derive
a simulation lemma for unbounded polynomial-length auxiliary
inputs assuming super-bit generators.
Index Terms—Cryptography, Proof systems, Verifiable computation, SNARKs.

I. I NTRODUCTION
Succinct non-interactive arguments (SNARGs) allow a prover
to convince a verifier of the truth of a statement through a short,
single-round message. The standard setting for SNARGs is the
common reference string (CRS) model, where a trusted setup
algorithm generates a CRS and shares it with both the prover
and the verifier. SNARGs have a wide range of applications,
including delegation of computation [1], verifying distributed
computation [2], [3], private information retrieval [4], zeroknowledge [5], blockchain [6]. Beyond cryptography, it has
been used to establish the cryptographic hardness of PPAD
[7]–[10].
Following the seminal work of Micali [11], which constructed SNARGs in the random oracle model, a long line
of research [12]–[23] has aimed to construct SNARGs from
well-studied, falsifiable hardness assumptions [24]. Notably,
it is known how to build SNARGs for NP under wellstudied cryptographic assumptions such as indistinguishability

obfuscation [25]–[28] or witness encryption with polynomialsize Extended Frege proof of correctness [29]. However, all
prior constructions of SNARGs for NP from well-studied
assumptions have a long CRS whose length grows with the
NP witness size. This leads to the following question:
Is there any fundamental barrier to constructing SNARGs for
NP from standard assumptions,
with a short CRS whose length is sublinear in the witness
size?
A short CRS is a natural requirement of succinctness in
SNARGs. In practice, SNARGs typically require a distributed
“ceremony” protocol to generate the CRS. A shorter CRS
can reduce the cost of this setup phase and also improve the
efficiency of the prover and verifier.
a) Gentry-Wichs Barrier: Previously, the seminal work
by Gentry and Wichs [30] showed that SNARGs for NP cannot
be constructed from any falsifiable assumptions, assuming a
black-box soundness reduction and the SNARG is adaptively
sound. As observed in [31], if the reduction preserves the
security parameter of the underlying falsifiable assumption, the
Gentry–Wichs impossibility result also applies in the long CRS
setting. However, Gentry-Wichs impossibility result crucially
relies on adaptive soundness, where the cheating prover may
choose the instance after observing the CRS.
b) This Work: Non-adaptive Soundness: In this work, we
investigate whether any inherent barrier still exists in the nonadaptive soundness setting. In this setting, the CRS is generated
independently of the instance selected by the adversary. This is
a weaker notion than adaptive soundness, as it is implied by the
latter. Nevertheless, non-adaptive soundness suffices for many
applications in which the instance is chosen independently of
the CRS. Moreover, non-adaptive soundness can be generically
upgraded to adaptive soundness using complexity leveraging,
although this comes at the cost of increasing the proof length
with the instance size.
This leads to the central question of this work:
Is there an inherent barrier to constructing SNARGs for NP
with a short CRS
that satisfy non-adaptive soundness from falsifiable
assumptions?

c) Updatable SNARGs (i.e. IVC for NP): Updatable
SNARGs are defined in the following setting. Consider a
nondeterministic computation st0 → st1 → st2 → . . . → st𝑇 ,
where in the 𝑖-th step, one runs a nondeterministic machine
with some witness 𝑤 𝑖 on the current state st𝑖 and produces
the next state st𝑖+1 . We say a SNARG is updatable, if given
the initial state st0 , a state st𝑖 , a proof 𝜋 𝑖 that st𝑖 is reachable
via 𝑖-step nondeterministic computation, and the 𝑖-th witness
𝑤 𝑖 , the prover can efficiently transform 𝜋 𝑖 into a proof 𝜋 𝑖+1
that the state st𝑖+1 is reachable via a (𝑖 + 1)-step computation,
without recomputing everything from scratch.
This notion was initially introduced for proving deterministic
computation and is known as incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) [2]. Recently, IVC has been implicitly extended
to support nondeterministic computation in concretely efficient
IVC schemes [33]–[36], and the recent work [37] constructed
IVC for NP with CRS length growing with the single-step
witness from standard assumptions.
In the broader context, the updatable feature of SNARGs has
been extensively studied for verifying distributed computation.
Indeed, it can be viewed as a special case of proof-carrying
data [3] and recursive composition [38]. These techniques
are particularly attractive for concretely efficient SNARG
constructions (e.g. [39], [40]), as their prover preserves the
time and space complexity of the underlying computation, and
is a common “bootstrap” technique to reduce the CRS size
[38]. The impossibility we obtain in the updatable setting also
implies the impossibility of those more general settings.
In this work, we focus on updatable SNARGs whose
CRS length and proof length are both succinct, smaller than
intermediate states size or length of single-step witnesses. We
consider non-adaptive soundness for updatable SNARGs, where
the initial state and the final state of the computation must be
chosen independently of the CRS.

Falsifiable assumptions [24] are assumptions that can be
formulated as an interactive game between a challenger and
an adversary. In this framework, the challenger generates
a challenge, and the adversary attempts to solve it. The
assumption is considered falsifiable, if the challenger runs in
polynomial-time—so any successful adversary serves as a piece
of evidence against the assumption. All standard cryptographic
assumptions—such as factoring or Learning With Errors—are
captured by falsifiable assumptions.
a) Non-Uniform Reduction: Our Theorem I.1 focuses on
uniform soundness reductions. We then turn to the question
of whether any inherent barrier remains when allowing nonuniform reductions. In this setting, the reduction algorithm
is allowed to take non-uniform advice—an arbitrary string
that may depend on the instance, but independent of the
adversary. Indeed, recent work [29], [32] has shown that nonadaptively sound SNARGs can be achieved by using nonuniform reductions for some subclasses of NP from standard
assumptions. In the setting of non-uniform reductions, we
consider general SNARGs and obtain the following theorem:
Theorem I.3 (Impossibility for General SNARGs, Informal).
Assuming the existence of a sub-exponentially secure superbit generator, there does not exist a SNARG for NP that
satisfies non-adaptive soundness, has a CRS whose length is
independent of the length of the instance and witness, and has
a 1-query polynomial-time black-box non-uniform soundness
reduction to falsifiable assumptions.
Our result relies on the existence of super-bit generators.
Rudich introduced the super-bit generator as a natural extension
of pseudorandom generators secure against NP adversaries,
in the context of the natural proofs barrier [41]. The superbit generator can be viewed as an average-case analog of the
widely believed complexity conjecture coNP ⊈ NP. In his
original work, Rudich proposed a candidate construction based
on the subset-sum problem. Recently, [42] proposed another
candidate of super-bit generators based on lattice assumptions.
b) On 1-Query Reductions: Our Theorem I.3 considers
reduction algorithms that only make one query to the adversary.

Gentry-Wichs also applies in the long CRS setting when the
CRS can grow with the NP instance length and witness length.
All of our results, by contrast, assume that the CRS length is

II. T ECHNICAL OVERVIEW
Before diving into the technical details of this work, we
briefly recall the Gentry–Wichs impossibility result [30], which
showed that adaptive soundness of SNARGs cannot be based
on falsifiable assumptions via black-box reductions.
A. Recap of Gentry-Wichs Barrier
A black-box soundness reduction is an algorithm ℛ that
uses a hypothetical adversary 𝒫 as an oracle to break the
underlying falsifiable assumption. As a black-box reduction,
the algorithm ℛ𝒫 should break the assumption as long as 𝒫
breaks the soundness of the SNARG, regardless of whether 𝒫
is efficient.
At a high level, Gentry-Wichs rules out such a black-box
reduction for adaptively sound SNARGs via the following
“meta-reduction” strategy. They construct a pair of adversaries
𝒫 and 𝒫 where 𝒫 is a polynomial-time algorithm that always
chooses instances that are in the language and follows the
honest prover algorithm, whereas 𝒫 runs in unbounded time
and chooses instances that are not in the language. Moreover,
for any CRS, the outputs of the two adversaries 𝒫 and 𝒫 are
indistinguishable against any polynomial-time algorithm.
To rule out black-box reductions, they start with the “honest”
prover 𝒫 that always makes the verifier accept. Then they
switch 𝒫 to 𝒫 and argue that 𝒫 breaks the soundness. This
is because 𝒫 and 𝒫 are indistinguishable and hence, 𝒫 also
makes the verifier accept, but chooses instances that are not in
the language. Further, the correctness of the reduction implies
that ℛ𝒫 breaks the underlying falsifiable assumption. Finally,
they switch ℛ𝒫 back to ℛ𝒫 and argue that ℛ𝒫 still breaks the
underlying assumption, again due to the indistinguishability
of 𝒫 and 𝒫. This reaches a contradiction because we find a
polynomial-time attack ℛ𝒫 to break the underlying falsifiable
assumption.

B. Impossibility for Updatable SNARGs
a) Challenge: Ruling Out “Rewinding” Reductions: The
proof strategy in Gentry-Wichs works for adaptive soundness.
However, it is unclear how to extend the idea to the nonadaptive soundness setting. In this setting, after the adversary
chooses the instance, the reduction algorithm can send different
CRS queries to the adversary and obtain multiple SNARG
proofs for the same instance. The reduction algorithm could
potentially extract an entire witness from the adversary and
then prove the soundness by a proof of contradiction. This
resembles the rewinding technique in multi-round interactive
proof soundness proofs. 2 To extend Gentry-Wichs to the
non-adaptive soundness setting, we need to rule out such a
rewinding proof strategy.
b) Blueprint of Our Proof: Our intuition to rule out
the above rewinding reduction strategy is that, for a general
NP language, if an instance has multiple witnesses, then the
rewinding strategy seems unlikely to work——if an honest
prover chooses different witnesses based on different CRS each
time, then it’s unclear how to “stitch” the information from
different SNARG proofs to form a consistent NP witness in
the reduction.
Following this intuition, our blueprint for proving impossibility in the non-adaptive soundness setting is as follows.
We first choose an NP language ℒ where each instance in ℒ
has multiple NP witnesses. Then we construct a polynomialtime algorithm 𝒫 for an instance 𝑥 ∈ ℒ sampled from some
distribution. Given any CRS queried by the reduction, 𝒫
randomly chooses a witness of 𝑥 and uses the honest prover
algorithm to generate an SNARG proof as its output. Next,
we use a series of hybrid arguments to “gradually” switch
from 𝒫 to an unbounded-time adversary 𝒫 for an instance
𝑥¯ ∉ ℒ, such that any polynomial-time oracle-algorithm 𝐷
cannot distinguish 𝐷 𝒫 and 𝐷 𝒫 . The number of hybrids is the
same as the number of NP witnesses for 𝑥. In each hybrid,
we “remove” one witness from 𝑥, and replace the honestly
generated SNARG proof of this witness with a simulated proof
using Gentry-Wichs’ leakage lemma.

C. Impossibility for General SNARGs
In this section, we focus on general non-adaptively sound
SNARGs, without assuming any additional feature of the
prover’s algorithm. We outline the techniques in our Theorem I.3, which rules out 1-query non-uniform black-box
reductions in this setting.
a) Non-uniform Reduction and Non-deterministic Computation: In a non-uniform reduction, the reduction algorithm is
additionally given a polynomially long advice that arbitrarily
depends on the instance. Since the 1-query to the adversary
can always be simulated if the language is “hard” enough,
as shown in Gentry-Wichs’ leakage lemma, we can ignore
this 1-query for the moment. Under this view, the reduction
algorithm is essentially a nondeterministic algorithm, where
the non-uniform advice can be viewed as the NP witness.
To rule out non-uniform reductions, we need to choose a
hard language ℒ that can fool this nondeterministic reduction
algorithm. A natural candidate is the super-bit generators introduced in [53] as the analogue of PRG against nondeterministic
distinguishers. The security of super-bit generators guarantees
that, any nondeterministic algorithm accepts a random string
with no noticeably higher probability than accepting a random
super-bit generator image. Intuitively, this assumption can be
viewed as saying “uniformly random strings” do not have

NP proofs “on average”. Note that in the nondeterministic
setting, indistinguishability is directional. While we believe
the existence of super-bit generator, it is easy to construct a
nondeterministic algorithm that accepts a random super-bit
generator image with higher probability than a random string:
the algorithm just checks if the input is in the image of the
super-bit generator. Because of this reason, in the rest of this
section we adopt the notation “𝑋 → 𝑌 are indistinguishable”
(which means 𝑋 cannot be accepted with noticeably higher
probability than 𝑌) rather than “𝑋 , 𝑌 are indistinguishable” to
stress the order between distributions 𝑋 , 𝑌.
We can let the hard language ℒ be the set of the images of

D. One-query Nature of Existing SNARG Reductions
We briefly sketch why the security reductions in many recent
SNARG constructions are essentially one-query.
The high level intuition is, these reductions are structurally
simple: they are composed of multiple 1-query reductions to
search or decision problems. We batch these reductions into
a 1-query reduction by randomly selecting one to perform. A
caveat lies in batching reductions to decision problems: the
distinguishing advantage may cancel out each other. Fortunately,
reductions to decision problems usually come from hybrid
arguments, for which the security proofs only concern the
increasement of the adversary’s success probability, that is, the
hybrid arguments only concern one-side indistinguishability.
This property enables us to avoid the “cancelling out” issue.
In the following, we examine several popular SNARG
constructions, including hash-and-BARG SNARGs (to name a
few, [19], [32], [43]) and Sahai-Waters SNARGs [25].
